title: Prithu asks for ten thousand ears
hookLine: a king offered any boon turns down liberation
carry: pure bhakti makes even liberation look light
tomorrow: a mother's rope keeps coming up two fingers short. why?

cards: In the Bhagavata Purana, King Prithu has just come through a bitter quarrel with Indra, king of the gods, over a stolen sacrificial horse.
The quarrel is calmed, and Vishnu himself arrives, with Indra beside him, and stands before Prithu, pleased. Ask for a boon, he says. Here's what makes the story well-known.
Prithu doesn't ask for a longer reign or a safer kingdom. He doesn't even ask for moksha, liberation from the cycle of birth and death, which many Hindu schools name the goal past every goal.
In paraphrase he says: I don't want even that liberation, if there's no hearing about you in it. Give me ten thousand ears. Why would anyone turn down the finish line?

teach.b: Rupa answers in his list of what pure bhakti does. In paraphrase: it ends suffering. It brings what is good.
It makes liberation seem light. It is very hard to come by. It is a joy that is dense and of a special kind.
And it draws Krishna himself. The first marks are what anyone might hope from a spiritual path. Then the turn.
A devotee who has tasted that dense joy isn't looking for the exit, because the exit was never the prize.
The love is. That's Prithu's ten thousand ears: he'd rather keep hearing about Vishnu forever than be finished.

The Bhagavata says it again elsewhere: the Lord, teaching as the sage Kapila, speaks of devotees who won't accept liberation, even when it's offered, if it comes without serving him. And the last mark is the boldest.
Bhakti doesn't only carry the devotee toward God. In this lineage, love pulls God toward the devotee. This is a real fork in Hindu thought.
For many schools, moksha stays the highest aim, and later this week the track hears one of them, with Shankara. Rupa's book says plainly where it stands.
Gaudiya devotees pray for loving service, life after life, not for the exit.

how: In Gaudiya Vaishnava teaching, these marks of pure bhakti are read as signs to recognize, and devotees speak of loving service, not liberation, as what they hope for. Hearing Krishna's stories and singing his names together is a central daily practice.

games.q: what does “rupa goswami's bhakti rasamrita sindhu” mean?
o: a story of a river's journey to the sea
a book that lists what pure bhakti does
a guide to winning moksha by austerity

games.q: the marks of pure bhakti. tap the pairs.
p: ten thousand ears, to keep hearing
dense, and of a special kind

s: every Hindu path aims at the same final goal, moksha
for some schools moksha stays the highest aim; in Rupa's book, pure bhakti makes even liberation look light.
in Rupa's list, bhakti carries the devotee to God but never draws God
the last mark is the boldest: pure bhakti draws Krishna himself.
Rupa says pure bhakti is very hard to come by
it's one of the marks on his list, alongside the dense, special joy.

games.q: in the Bhagavata Purana, the Lord, teaching as the sage Kapila, speaks of devotees offered liberation, but it would come without serving him. what do they do?
o: they take it gladly; it's the goal.
they ask to serve first, then take it.
games.why: The passage says such devotees won't accept liberation, even offered, if it comes without serving the Lord. For them the love is the prize.

practice: Put on one devotional song, a bhajan or a kirtan your family plays, or hum one you remember, and give it the whole of your hearing, with nothing else open. If you pray, let it be Prithu's prayer: one more hearing.
If you don't, just notice the moment you stop waiting for it to end.

wordCard.voice: Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu: a book that lists what pure bhakti does, up to making liberation seem light and drawing Krishna close.

orig.note: Sanskrit moksha, liberation from the cycle of birth and death; Rupa says pure bhakti makes even this seem light.

carryVoice: For the road: pure bhakti makes even liberation look light. Prithu asked for ears, not the exit. Day sixteen sixty-eight, done.

sources.ref: Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.1.17 (the marks of pure bhakti: ends suffering, gives good, makes liberation light, very rare, dense joy, draws Krishna)

Bhagavata Purana 4.20 (Vishnu, arriving with Indra after the quarrel over Prithu's sacrificial horse, offers Prithu a boon; Prithu declines even liberation without hearing of Vishnu and asks for ten thousand ears, around 4.20.24)
Bhagavata Purana 3.29.13 (the Lord as Kapila to his mother Devahuti: devotees do not accept liberation, though offered, without service to him)
